blocks.prompt: The Ball Made of Shapes
blocks.text: Pick up a classic soccer ball and count the patches on its surface. You will find thirty-two of them. Twenty are white and have six sides each. Twelve are black and have five sides each. Shapes with six sides are called hexagons. Shapes with five sides are called pentagons. When these flat pieces are stitched together, they pull the ball into a smooth round shape. The black pentagons were not just for looks. This design first appeared at the World Cup in 1970. Back then, many families watched the games on black-and-white televisions. A plain white ball was hard to follow on the screen. The black patches made the ball easy to see, and they helped players and fans watch how the ball was spinning as it flew through the air. Before this ball, teams played with brown leather balls. Those balls grew heavy in the rain and could hurt your head.

blocks.prompt: The Shape Hiding Inside the Ball
blocks.text: A soccer ball looks perfectly round, but it is built from flat pieces that only pretend to be curved. The classic ball has thirty-two panels: twenty white hexagons, each with six sides, and twelve black pentagons, each with five sides. Mathematicians have a name for this arrangement. They call it a truncated icosahedron, which is a fancy way of saying a twenty-sided shape with its corners sliced off. Each cut corner becomes a pentagon, and the flat faces become hexagons. When air fills the ball and pushes the panels outward, the sharp edges soften and the whole thing rounds into a sphere. This exact ball became famous at the 1970 World Cup, where it was called the Telstar. Its black patches were a clever idea. Most people at home were still watching on black-and-white televisions, and a solid white ball almost vanished against the pale field. The dark pentagons gave viewers something to track, so they could finally see the ball curve and spin. Soccer balls were not always so clever. The earliest ones were animal bladders blown up with air. Later, people wrapped leather around the bladder to make it tougher. Leather worked well in dry weather, but it drank up rain like a sponge. A soaked leather ball could become so heavy that heading it was dangerous. Modern balls solve this with waterproof synthetic panels and a sealed rubber bladder inside, so they stay light no matter the weather.

blocks.prompt: The Ball That Is Really a Solid
blocks.text: Hold a classic soccer ball still and study it as an object, not a toy. What you are holding is a piece of geometry that people have admired for more than two thousand years. Its surface is made of thirty-two flat panels: twenty hexagons with six sides each and twelve pentagons with five sides each. Every pentagon is surrounded entirely by hexagons, and no two pentagons ever touch. This precise pattern has a name that ancient Greek thinkers already knew: the truncated icosahedron. You can build it by taking a twenty-sided solid and slicing off each of its twelve corners. The old corners leave behind pentagons, and the original faces open into hexagons. The same shape shows up in surprising places. In 1985, scientists discovered a molecule made of sixty carbon atoms arranged in exactly this pattern. They named it buckminsterfullerene, after an architect who built dome-shaped buildings from the same geometry, and nicknamed it the buckyball. A soccer ball, a carbon molecule, and a domed roof all share one design because it is a remarkably strong and balanced way to wrap a curved surface with flat pieces. Turning that geometry into a ball you can kick took centuries of invention. The earliest balls were animal bladders, later covered in leather for toughness. Leather soaked up rain and grew dangerously heavy. A real breakthrough came in the 1800s, when Charles Goodyear used a process called vulcanization to make rubber that stayed springy in heat and cold. Rubber bladders held their air far better than animal ones. The famous thirty-two-panel design arrived in the twentieth century and was chosen for the 1970 World Cup, where its black patches helped fans follow the ball on black-and-white televisions. Modern balls have quietly moved on from that classic pattern. Engineers found that the number and shape of the panels change how the ball moves through the air. Fewer panels, or oddly shaped ones, can make a ball swerve unpredictably, which is why some tournament balls have caused arguments among goalkeepers. The rounder and smoother the surface, the harder it becomes to guess where a fast, spinning shot will end up.

blocks.prompt: Forever Round: The Hidden Geometry of the Soccer Ball
blocks.text: A soccer ball may be the most widely recognized object on Earth, and almost nobody notices that it is a lie. It looks like a sphere, but it is not one. It is a polyhedron, a solid built entirely from flat faces, that only becomes round when air pressure pushes its panels outward and stretches the flatness away. The classic version carries thirty-two panels: twenty hexagons of six sides and twelve pentagons of five sides, arranged so that every pentagon is ringed by hexagons and no two pentagons meet. Geometers call this figure a truncated icosahedron. Begin with an icosahedron, a twenty-faced solid the ancient Greeks catalogued, then shave off each of its twelve corners. The severed corners leave pentagons, the widened faces become hexagons, and you arrive at a shape with sixty corners and ninety edges that balances flat pieces around a curve better than almost any alternative. That efficiency is why the same pattern keeps reappearing far from any sports field. In 1985 chemists found a molecule of sixty carbon atoms locked into this exact arrangement. They named it buckminsterfullerene, after the architect Buckminster Fuller, whose geodesic domes used the same principle, and the discovery later earned a Nobel Prize. Scientists still call the molecule a buckyball, because a soccer ball is the clearest picture of what it looks like. The object itself is the result of a long argument with the weather. The earliest balls were inflated animal bladders, fragile and lopsided. Wrapping them in leather made them tougher but introduced a fatal weakness: leather absorbs water, and a rain-soaked ball could double in weight and injure a player heading it. The turning point was vulcanization, the process Charles Goodyear developed in the 1800s to make rubber that stayed elastic in both heat and cold. A sealed rubber bladder finally held its shape and its air. The thirty-two-panel ball most people picture was popularized as the Telstar at the 1970 World Cup, its black pentagons chosen so that viewers watching on black-and-white televisions could track the spin. Then engineers started tampering with tradition, and physics pushed back. A ball with fewer panels has fewer seams, and seams are what grip the air and steady a ball in flight. The 2010 World Cup ball, built from only eight bonded panels, flew so unpredictably that goalkeepers publicly complained it swerved and dipped without warning. The culprit was a phenomenon called knuckling: when a ball spins very little, its smooth surface lets the air cling and release in erratic bursts, and the ball wobbles off course. The 2014 replacement added carefully shaped seams to tame the effect. It turns out that the humble stitched pattern was never only decoration. Those thirty-two panels were doing quiet, invisible work, holding a fast ball honest as it cut through the air.
